definition: Inchoate means just begun and not yet fully formed.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inchoate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inchoate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The rebellion was still inchoate — muttered grievances, one stolen map, and no plan worth the name.
Unpolished work is essentially finished and needs only smoothing — it stops well short of inchoate on this scale of rawness.
Sketchy work has an outline but thin details — it still stops short of inchoate, which has no settled shape at all.

Unformed means not yet given shape — clay still a lump, a plan still a mood — with the expectation that shaping lies ahead. Inchoate adds one thing: the shaping has actually started. An inchoate theory is under construction; an unformed one is still waiting.

Formless means having no shape at all, and possibly never meant to have one — drifting smoke, radio static. Inchoate points the other way: an inchoate thing has begun moving toward a form, however far it still has to travel.

Inchoate rides on Latin cohum, the strap that yoked a plow team — incohare, 'to hitch up,' hence 'to begin.' English never borrowed cohum into any other word, so inchoate stands alone; even the lawyers' jokey back-formation 'choate' is a made-up opposite, not a real relative.
Inchoate means just begun and not yet fully formed.
An architect's first massing model is foam blocks on a board: no doors, no windows, no stairs.
She calls the design inchoate on purpose — too early for details, and honest about it.
Inchoate says the thing exists but hasn't found its shape.
Its neighbor incipient (this unit) points at the calendar — just beginning; inchoate points at the form — not yet formed.
Latin incohare meant 'to hitch up the plow team': work barely begun, oxen still being strapped in.
Inchoate is for things that exist but haven't found their form — plans, theories, feelings.
Incipient (this unit) marks how early a thing is; inchoate marks how shapeless.
In everyday talk, half-formed or rough does the work.

Every biography of the aviation pioneer Bess Corman lingers on the winter of 1921, when her airline was still inchoate.
It existed, but barely: a borrowed hangar, a single leased biplane, and a route map drawn in pencil on the back of a feed-store calendar.
Investors who visited saw chaos.
Corman saw a beginning — the first pieces of a shape only she could make out.
Her diary from those months repeats one entry like a drumbeat: 'Not nothing anymore.
Not yet something.' Within four years the pencil route map had hardened into printed timetables, and the company she had argued into existence flew mail over three states.
